stem: The Asiatic Society of Bengal, founded in 1784 to study Indian languages and culture, was established by:
solution: William Jones, an Orientalist scholar, founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal in 1784 and studied Sanskrit, Persian and Arabic texts.

stem: Scholars like William Jones who admired and wished to promote Indian languages and learning were called:
solution: Orientalists respected Indian classical languages and traditions and favoured promoting Sanskrit, Persian and Arabic learning.

stem: The Calcutta Madrasa, set up in 1781 to promote the study of Arabic, Persian and Islamic law, was established under:
solution: The Calcutta Madrasa was set up in 1781 during Warren Hastings' time to encourage the study of Arabic, Persian and Islamic law.

stem: The Hindu College at Benares (1791), for the study of ancient Sanskrit texts, was established by:
solution: Jonathan Duncan set up the Benares Sanskrit College in 1791 to promote the study of Hindu law and philosophy.

stem: The famous 'Minute on Education' (1835) that strongly advocated English education was written by:
solution: Thomas Macaulay's 1835 Minute argued for English-medium education and dismissed Indian learning, shaping colonial education policy.

stem: Macaulay's aim was to create a class of people who would be 'Indian in blood and colour, but ________ in taste, opinions and intellect.'
solution: Macaulay wanted to create Indians who were English in taste, opinions, morals and intellect, to serve as intermediaries.

stem: Following Macaulay's Minute, the English Education Act was passed in:
solution: The English Education Act of 1835 made English the medium of higher education and stopped the promotion of Oriental institutions.

stem: The 1854 educational despatch that laid out a comprehensive scheme of education in India is known as:
solution: Wood's Despatch (1854), from Charles Wood, outlined a system of education from primary to university level and is called the 'Magna Carta of English education in India'.

stem: Wood's Despatch of 1854 is often described as the:
options: Magna Carta of English education in India
solution: Because it set out the framework of the modern education system, Wood's Despatch is called the 'Magna Carta of English education in India'.

stem: Following Wood's Despatch, the first three modern universities in India were set up in 1857 at:
solution: The universities of Calcutta, Madras and Bombay were established in 1857 as a result of Wood's Despatch.

stem: Traditional Indian village schools were known as:
solution: Pathshalas were the indigenous village schools, often run by a single teacher (guru), providing flexible local education.

stem: A distinctive feature of the traditional pathshala system was that it had:
options: Fixed fees, printed books, classrooms and annual exams
No fixed fees, no benches, no separate classes or examinations, with flexible timings
solution: Pathshalas were flexible — no rigid fees, classrooms, benches, printed textbooks or exams; teaching adjusted to local needs and seasons.

stem: The person whose report in the 1830s described the pathshalas of Bengal and Bihar was:
solution: William Adam surveyed and reported on the vast network of pathshalas in Bengal and Bihar in the 1830s.

stem: After deciding to 'improve' the pathshala system, the Company:
options: Introduced rules, appointed government pandits/inspectors, and imposed routines, reducing their flexibility
Abolished all of them at once
Handed them over to missionaries only
solution: The Company tried to regulate pathshalas — appointing inspectors, prescribing routines and textbooks — which curtailed their earlier flexibility.

stem: Mahatma Gandhi criticised English/colonial education mainly because he felt it:
options: Created a sense of inferiority and enslaved Indians, cutting them off from their own culture
solution: Gandhi argued that colonial education instilled a sense of inferiority, alienated Indians from their surroundings and made them look up to British ways.

stem: Rabindranath Tagore founded which centre of learning, emphasising creativity and closeness to nature?
solution: Tagore founded Shantiniketan in 1901, promoting natural, creative and joyful learning free from rigid discipline.

stem: Gandhi believed that education should be imparted primarily in:
solution: Gandhi favoured education in the mother tongue and stressed practical knowledge and handicrafts over bookish English learning.

stem: The 'Anglicists' in the education debate argued that:
options: Indian classical learning should be promoted
European/English learning and science should be taught to Indians
solution: Anglicists like Macaulay held that Western knowledge and the English language should form the basis of education in India.

stem: The idea behind the British 'civilising mission' in education was that:
options: The British had a duty to 'civilise' Indians by spreading Western knowledge and values
solution: The 'civilising mission' assumed Indian culture was inferior and that it was the British duty to civilise Indians through Western education.

stem: Gandhi felt that Western education emphasised reading and writing over:
options: Practical knowledge, craft and the dignity of manual work
solution: Gandhi valued learning a craft and the dignity of manual labour, which he felt colonial education neglected in favour of mere literacy.

stem: The Orientalist scholars believed that to win the trust of Indians and rule effectively, the British should:
options: Learn and engage with India's own laws, languages and sacred texts
solution: Orientalists argued that understanding Indian laws, languages and scriptures would help the British govern with the people's cooperation.

stem: The Serampore Mission and other missionaries contributed to education by:
options: Setting up printing presses and schools
solution: Missionaries such as those at Serampore set up printing presses and schools, spreading education (and Christianity).

stem: Which of the following best states James Mill's view on Indian education?
options: Indians should be taught useful, practical Western knowledge, not just Oriental literature
solution: James Mill argued that education should teach Indians useful, practical Western knowledge rather than 'flowery' Oriental literature.

stem: One reason the Company initially supported Oriental learning was that it:
options: Wanted to win the goodwill of Indian scholars and rule with their cooperation
solution: Early on, supporting Indian classical learning was seen as a way to gain the respect and cooperation of learned Indians.

stem: The pathshala teacher who taught students was called the:
solution: The pathshala was run by a guru (teacher) who taught pupils according to local needs and seasons.

stem: Which pair is correctly matched?
solution: William Jones was an Orientalist; Macaulay was the leading Anglicist. Tagore stood for a creative Indian model of education.

stem: Wood's Despatch argued that European learning would benefit Indians by:
options: Improving their morals and making them useful, along with commercial benefits for Britain
solution: Wood's Despatch claimed European education would improve Indians' 'moral character' and provide reliable workers, while also expanding markets for British goods.

stem: A key criticism of colonial education by Indian thinkers was that its curriculum was:
options: Foreign, bookish and disconnected from Indian life and needs
solution: Indian critics felt colonial education was alien, overly literary and detached from Indian realities, needs and culture.

stem: The English Education Act of 1835 resulted in the Company stopping funds for:
options: The promotion of Oriental institutions and printing of Sanskrit/Arabic works
solution: After 1835, the Company diverted resources to English education and stopped promoting Oriental (Sanskrit/Arabic/Persian) learning.

stem: The overall aim of British education policy, as it developed, was to:
options: Produce a large class of Indians trained in English to help run the administration
solution: The policy aimed to create a class of English-educated Indians to serve as clerks and intermediaries in the colonial administration.

stem: Tagore's Shantiniketan reflected his belief that childhood should be a time of:
options: Self-learning, creativity and freedom, close to nature
solution: Tagore wanted children to learn freely and creatively in a natural environment, rejecting the rigid discipline of colonial schools.

stem: The 'vernacular' education debate concerned teaching in:
solution: Vernacular education referred to teaching in Indian regional languages, an issue debated alongside English-medium instruction.

stem: The traditional flexibility of pathshalas meant that classes were often adjusted to:
options: The needs of the harvest and local seasons
solution: Pathshala teaching was flexible, pausing during harvests so that children of peasant families could help in the fields.

stem: The British effort to 'civilise the native' assumed that Indian society was:
options: Backward and in need of European improvement
solution: The colonial 'civilising' project rested on the belief that Indian society was backward and needed to be reformed on European lines.

stem: The introduction of printed textbooks and fixed exams under colonial reforms affected pathshalas by:
options: Standardising and disciplining them, reducing the guru's freedom to adapt teaching
solution: Standardised texts, routines and inspections regularised pathshalas but took away the guru's earlier freedom to shape teaching locally.

stem: Which statement about William Jones is correct?
options: He learned Sanskrit and admired ancient Indian legal and literary texts
He wanted to abolish Indian languages
solution: William Jones learned Sanskrit and deeply admired classical Indian literature and law, founding the Asiatic Society to study them.

stem: According to Gandhi, colonial schools mainly benefited the British by producing Indians who:
options: Admired British rule and served its administration
solution: Gandhi held that colonial education created Indians who admired the British and were useful to colonial administration, weakening national self-respect.

stem: The debate between Orientalists and Anglicists was ultimately about:
options: Whether to educate Indians in their classical traditions or in Western/English knowledge
solution: The core question was whether education should be based on India's classical languages and learning (Orientalists) or on Western knowledge in English (Anglicists).

stem: Which of the following institutions was set up by Orientalists?
solution: The Calcutta Madrasa (1781) and Benares Sanskrit College (1791) were Orientalist institutions; the 1857 universities followed the Anglicist Wood's Despatch.

stem: Charles Wood, who authored the 1854 Despatch, was the:
options: President of the Board of Control of the East India Company
solution: Charles Wood was the President of the Board of Control of the East India Company when he issued the famous Despatch of 1854.

stem: The overall consequence of colonial education policy was the emergence of:
options: A Western-educated Indian middle class, some of whom later led the national movement
The end of all Indian languages
solution: Colonial education produced a Western-educated middle class; ironically, many of them went on to lead the movement against British rule.

stem: The main reason the British wanted educated Indians was to:
options: Fill lower administrative and clerical posts cheaply
solution: English-educated Indians could staff the vast lower bureaucracy cheaply, which the British administration needed.

stem: Which of the following best describes the Orientalist attitude to Indian knowledge?
options: Respect and a wish to preserve and study it
solution: Orientalists respected India's classical heritage and sought to study and preserve its languages and texts.

stem: The title of the chapter, 'Civilising the Native, Educating the Nation', highlights the tension between:
options: Colonial ideas of 'improving' Indians and Indian ideas of an education suited to national needs
solution: The chapter contrasts the colonial 'civilising' agenda with Indian visions (Gandhi, Tagore) of education rooted in national culture and needs.

stem: Which of the following did NOT support English-medium education?
solution: William Jones was an Orientalist who valued Indian classical learning; Macaulay, Wood and Mill promoted Western/English education.

stem: By emphasising English education, the colonial state also sought to:
options: Spread European values and secure loyal intermediaries
solution: English education helped spread European ideas and values and produced a class of loyal, useful intermediaries for the colonial system.

stem: Gandhi's model of 'basic education' (Nai Talim) stressed:
options: Learning through productive craft/work and the mother tongue
solution: Gandhi's Nai Talim linked learning to productive craftwork and used the mother tongue, aiming at self-reliance and dignity of labour.

stem: The system of pathshalas declined under colonial rule mainly because:
options: The new standardised, funded system marginalised them and imposed rigid rules
solution: As the colonial state built a funded, standardised education system and imposed rules, the flexible pathshalas lost support and declined.

stem: The debates over education in colonial India were ultimately connected to the larger question of:
options: How to shape Indian minds and, later, the nation's future
solution: Education debates were about shaping how Indians thought and, in the nationalist view, about building an educated citizenry for a future nation.

stem: Under Gandhi's influence, education that combined learning with productive handicraft and used the mother tongue came to be called:
solution: Gandhi's scheme of 'Nai Talim' or Basic Education linked learning to a productive craft and the mother tongue, stressing self-reliance and dignity of labour.
